bridge: Builds on N06 HTTP framing, N04 byte streams, W01 proxy observations and C07 inconsistent state. Use paper transcripts first, then only the designated provider lab.
teaching:
A proxy and backend may parse the same bytes using different rules. If they disagree where one request ends, bytes one side treats as content may be treated as a subsequent request by the other. This is a protocol-composition defect, not merely a suspicious header name.

HTTP/1.1 framing includes defined rules for message body length and transfer coding. Production fixes require strict, consistent parsing and safe handling across every hop and protocol translation. Do not create a home-made parser or rely on blocking one sample string. HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1 translation introduces its own boundary considerations.

The exercise uses a deliberately abstract parser disagreement instead of a deployable smuggling payload. Record each parser's consumed range and the remaining bytes. This makes the mechanism understandable before a provider lab introduces exact version-specific protocol rules.
example:
Abstract fixture: byte positions0..19
Front parser assumes body ends after position9.
Back parser assumes body ends after position14.
Bytes10..14 are therefore interpreted differently.

Parser F: request1=[0..9], next begins10
Parser B: request1=[0..14], next begins15
Question: can both sides safely reuse this connection as if aligned?
explanation: The positions are a model, not valid HTTP syntax. The key evidence is inconsistent boundaries. A single application status code cannot by itself prove the exact parser path; a lab analysis needs controlled observations and knowledge of the proxy/backend chain.
exercise: Draw both boundary views for the supplied20-byte fixture. Then use matching end positions9/9 and explain the difference. State two requirements for a defensive proxy/backend configuration review.
solution: The mismatched model is desynchronised; the matched model agrees on the next-byte position. Review strict framing validation and consistent behaviour across hops/translation, plus rejection/connection handling for ambiguous messages.
challenge: Write a provider-lab evidence plan identifying scope, front/back protocol assumptions, baseline, one controlled variation, expected boundary effect and a safe stop condition. Explain why success against one parser version does not prove all deployments share the fault.
challenge_solution: Parsing and translation behaviour depend on actual components/configuration. Evidence must support the tested chain and avoid extrapolation. Do not send framing experiments to unrelated production sites.
